prompt: Write a ~700-word piece of literary short fiction about: the last week of a village post office. Prose only, no headings.
text:
The dust in the Oakhaven Post Office had settled into a permanent layer of beige silence for three weeks now, but today it felt different. It didn't just sit on the ledgers; it seemed to cling with an anticipatory weight, knowing that tomorrow morning would be its final day as such. Outside the window, the world moved in a rhythm that was indifferent to the building's expiration: leaves turned over under autumn winds, and children laughed down the gravel path where Mrs. Gable used to chase them for skipping stones near the counter. Inside, however, time had folded inward into itself, compressed by the looming closure date marked on every wall clock as if an invisible hand were trying to reverse their gears.

Elias, who would be retiring after forty years of service, stood behind the mahogany desk with a broom in his hand that looked more like a scepter than a cleaning tool. He swept not just dirt but history, moving from corner to corner where envelopes had accumulated over decades. The air smelled faintly of old paper, pipe tobacco residue, and lavender soap—the unique olfactory signature of Mrs. Gable's final week at the desk before her own retirement took effect two days prior. It was a scent that now hung heavy in the stagnant room, a perfume for an era ending too soon.

A young woman pushed through the door, shaking rain from her coat as she entered just after noon on Friday. She looked confused by the quietness of the place; there were no stacks of mail to sort, only two half-empty bins labeled "Outbound" and one small box marked for donation. "Is anyone here?" she called out, her voice echoing softly against bare walls where posters about postal rates had been stripped away weeks ago.

Elias paused mid-sweep and smiled at the intrusion with a warmth that seemed to defy the impending emptiness. "That's me," he said gently. He gestured for her to sit on the single wooden stool near the counter, though there was no work left to do. They talked about how the village had changed since she grew up in Oakhaven; now everyone ordered groceries online or sent text messages instead of handwritten notes. Elias listened with a tilt of his head that suggested he wasn't entirely sure if progress felt like advancement or loss. The young woman mentioned her mother, who lived an hour away and whom she hadn't seen in months because the bus schedule had shifted along with other municipal cuts.

"We still have to go out and meet people," Elias noted as they finished their tea from a chipped mug that would soon be packed into a cardboard box for charity shop donation. "That's what this place was always about." She nodded, though she knew he meant more than just the physical structure of the building; he meant the ritual of connection itself.

Saturday brought fewer visitors as news spread through town. Those who still held onto old habits came in batches to say goodbye before the last collection run on Sunday morning. There were tears shed over letters that would never make it across state lines, and a profound sense of grief for a community hub that had silently organized social life since the days when mail carriers walked every cobblestone street without fail. Even the elderly who could barely remember Elias's name came in to wave or leave small tokens left on the counter—a pressed flower from someone's garden, a polished stone found near the creek—all things preserved as artifacts of a simpler time.

On Sunday morning, it was just rain against glass and birdsong outside. The post office stood empty save for two figures arranging furniture into piles destined for auction or donation later that afternoon. As Elias packed away his stamp album—decades worth of cancelled stamps bearing the faces of presidents long forgotten by modern politics—he realized he felt a strange lightness in his chest, as if carrying the burden of closure finally allowed him to exhale after holding it too tight for forty years.

The door opened again on Sunday afternoon letting in slivers of grey light that danced across scattered paperwork and empty scales. A final group arrived: local teenagers with backpacks full of books rather than mailboxes; a few neighbors stopping by just out of habit before the realization set in fully what was happening to their town center today. They helped lift chairs onto trucks bound for storage units or second-hand shops, laughing nervously at how much effort it took simply to remove objects that belonged so deeply woven into daily life they hadn't noticed them until suddenly absent.

As dusk fell over Oakhaven casting long shadows across the wet pavement outside the closed post office windows inside which only dust motes danced in beams of fading sunlight Elias locked up carefully placing keys on a shelf marked "Closed Since Today" alongside photographs and memorabilia that would be kept safely intact somewhere else where stories might continue even if structures changed forever.
topic: the last week of a village post office
